newsitem.title: USA: Clinton courts votes in Bruce Springsteen's home town.
newsitem.headline: Clinton courts votes in Bruce Springsteen's home town.

text.p: President Bill Clinton campaigned in the hometown of working class rock idol Bruce Springsteen on Tuesday, seeking votes in a middle class New Jersey suburb with strong Republican leanings.

After signing the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty at a United Nations ceremony surrounded by pinstriped diplomats, Clinton addressed a decidedly different audience in the afternoon, with more T-shirts than ties in evidence.

Arriving at an outdoor campaign rally to the tune of a fife and drum corps, Clinton was saluted by supporters wearing Revolutionary War era uniforms and by loud cheers from a boisterous crowd of about 5,000.

Clinton used his speech to take aim at his Republican opponent Bob Dole, who trails him by double digits both nationally and in New Jersey, and to support Bob Torricelli, a Democratic congressman running for the Senate from the state.
In particular, the president sought to defend Torricelli, who was at his side, against Republican attacks for his support of Clinton's 1993 economic plan, which raised taxes.

Saying Torricelli "had the courage to put America's future over short-term demagoguery," Clinton said his economic plan had cut the deficit, lowered interest rates, created jobs and put the economy's health beyond argument.
"We'e better off today than we were four years ago. How could anybody dispute that," Clinton said to loud applause.

The U.S. Federal Reserve handed Clinton an election season gift earlier on Tuesday by leaving interest rates unchanged, an act that Clinton told reporters showed "we've got a strong economy with no inflation."

Clinton took a few shots at Dole in his speech, attacking the Republican for voting against the Family and Medical Leave Act, a popular law that lets people to take time off to care for newborns or sick family members.
"My distinguished opponent voted against the family leave law four times and said this year he still did the right thing," Clinton said.
"You hear people talking all the time about family values. Well, if we're going to talk about family values, should we value families?" he added.
A bellwether state in presidential politics, Clinton won New Jersey by two percentage points in 1992 while Republican George Bush carried the state in 1988.

A senior Clinton aide said the president came to the Freehold region, which voted narrowly for Bush in 1992, to court its traditionally conservative voters and to exploit scepticism about Dole plans for a 15 percent tax cut.

"There is more scepticism in this state about Bob Dole's tax cut than there is in most places," White House political director Doug Sosnik told reporters. "They don't belive he can actually do what he says he's going to do without increasing the deficit."
"They've heard the tax rap here for a long time," Sosnik added. "I think they have a pretty sophisticated understanding about when someone gives them something ... about how credible it is."

Clinton made no reference to rock star Springsteen in his speech, perhaps mindful of the singers's criticising former President Ronald Reagan for using his name in a 1984 New Jersey campain appearance.
While Springsteen was nowhere to be seen on Tuesday, he was certainly to be heard as the rally organisers played his songs to pump up the crowd before Clinton arrived.
